posts.style: Design & Aspiration · The Edge Is the View
posts.alt: A Del Mar hillside ocean-view estate backyard at sunset with a long vanishing-edge pool and a round stainless-rimmed spa, a wide ivory travertine deck, a linear gas fire trough along the pool edge, teak chaise loungers, a low board-formed concrete wall with warm uplights over agave and ornamental grasses, olive trees, and a limestone-clad contemporary home with glass doors open; neighboring Mediterranean and modern homes step down the hillside beside it toward the Pacific coastline
posts.hook: When the ocean is the view, the pool's only job is to get out of its way.
posts.caption:
On a coastal hillside, every element either frames the horizon or competes with it. There's no neutral.

So the pool runs parallel to the coastline and drops away at a vanishing edge — from the terrace the water simply meets the Pacific. The spa sits inside the water line, a clean stainless circle rather than a second hole in the deck. The fire runs as a single low line along the pool edge, warm at eye level without a single thing rising into the sightline. The planting stays low and silver against a board-formed wall, lit from beneath so the edge of the yard glows after sunset instead of disappearing.

A view like this doesn't need more design. It needs better restraint.

The selections:
• ivory travertine deck & coping
• vanishing-edge pool
• Diamond Spas stainless-steel spa
• Warming Trends linear fire trough
• board-formed concrete wall
• FX Luminaire uplighting · olive, agave & ornamental grasses

posts.style: Neighborhood · Driveway & Curb Appeal · Mid-Century, Respected
posts.alt: A mid-century modern home in Bay Park at golden hour with a low-pitched overhanging roof, clerestory windows, horizontal cedar siding and a teal front door, a wide charcoal Techo-Bloc paver driveway with a light-grey border band, large-format porcelain stepping pads floating over black beach pebbles to the entry, a stacked-stone raised planter with an olive tree, dragon trees, blue fescue and agave, low bronze path lights, and sailboat masts on Mission Bay in the distance
posts.hook: A mid-century house was designed in straight, quiet lines. The driveway should be too.
posts.caption:
These homes were drawn with discipline — long rooflines, clean planes, nothing extra. Most of them now sit behind a cracked slab and a strip of lawn that undo all of it.

This front yard goes back to the architecture. A charcoal paver field in a calm running bond, finished with a light border that squares the whole plane off to the street. The walk to the door becomes a series of large porcelain pads floating over black pebble, so the approach reads horizontal — just like the roofline above it. One stacked-stone planter anchors the corner with an olive and a few sculptural dragon trees, and low path lights carry the line to the entry after dark.

Nothing new competing with the house. Just the house, finally finished.

The selections:
• Techo-Bloc Industria pavers, running bond with contrast border
• large-format porcelain stepping pads
• black Mexican beach pebble
• Eldorado Stone ledgestone planter wall
• olive, dragon trees, blue fescue & agave
• FX Luminaire path lighting

posts.style: Process Carousel · Property Walk to Built
posts.alt: Four-slide SDLR process carousel of one Rancho Bernardo tract-home backyard between neighboring two-story tile-roof houses: the existing yard at the property walk with a cracked concrete slab and patchy dry lawn, the full 3D design render with louvered pergola, outdoor kitchen, fire pit and curving turf, a hand-rendered overhead design drawing of the same layout, and the finished build photographed at golden hour
posts.hook: Here's how a backyard goes from “we're not sure what to do with this” to built — without a single guess along the way.
posts.caption:
Most yards don't need more ideas. They need an order of operations — especially on a normal lot with neighbors ten feet away on either side.

Swipe through how our design process works, start to finish:

1. The property walk — we start with what's actually there. The slab, the grade, the sun, the view you want to keep and the one you don't.
2. The concept render — the whole space modeled in 3D, so you can see the kitchen, the pergola, the fire and the lawn in place and change anything before it's real.
3. The drawing — every edge, level and planting resolved on paper, so the crew builds exactly what you approved.
4. The build — and it matches, because nothing was left to be figured out in the field.

The render is the design. The last slide is the build. The whole point is that they look the same.

The selections:
• Techo-Bloc Blu 60 paver terrace
• StruXure louvered pergola
• Eldorado Stone outdoor kitchen with Lynx built-in grill & raised bar
• Warming Trends gas fire pit
• SYNLawn turf panel
• olive, agave & lavender in raised planters · FX Luminaire lighting

posts.style: Lifestyle · Every Age Has a Corner
posts.alt: A family backyard behind a sage-green board-and-batten two-story home with stone wainscot in Rancho San Diego at golden hour, with neighboring two-story stucco homes right next door over tan block walls and more homes on the hillside beyond; a paver patio, a curving turf putting green with flags, a round gas fire pit beside a curved cushioned stone seat wall, a white pergola with string lights over a dining table, terracotta pots with lemon trees, lavender and rosemary, and a wood deck in the foreground
posts.hook: The best family yards aren't one big space. They're four small ones that all work at once.
posts.caption:
The trick to a yard the whole family actually uses is giving everyone somewhere to be.

On a normal suburban lot, that means zones instead of one open slab. The putting green takes the long side, so someone's always sneaking in ten minutes of practice. The fire pit sits against a curved stone seat wall — built-in seating means no chairs to drag around and room for everyone when the sun drops. Dinner lives under the pergola and string lights, close enough to the kitchen door that eating outside is the default, not an event. Lemons and lavender in planters keep the edges soft and smell like California.

Kids, grandparents, a Thursday night. Everyone has a corner.

The selections:
• Belgard Urbana paver patio
• SYNLawn Golf putting green & SYNLawn turf
• Warming Trends CrossFire gas fire pit
• Eldorado Stone curved seat wall
• Trex Pergola with cafe string lights
• potted Meyer lemons, lavender & rosemary

posts.style: Trust & Difference · By Design, Not by Dispatch
posts.alt: A small coastal courtyard seen through open black steel French doors in Solana Beach, with neighboring board-and-batten and stucco homes rising just beyond the white stucco walls, palms over the rooftops, a copper water bowl spilling into river stones, large warm limestone-tone porcelain pavers with gravel joints, a white louvered pergola over teak chaise loungers, a stone bench with linen cushions, an olive tree, bougainvillea on the wall, rosemary and germander, and bronze path lights
posts.hook: A quiet yard isn't a smaller project. It's a more careful one.
posts.caption:
The calmest spaces are the ones where nothing was rushed. You can feel it the moment you step through the doors.

That's why we don't work by dispatch. Every project is planned before it's built and scheduled well ahead, so the design gets the time it needs: the joints between the pavers set to line up with the doors, the water bowl placed where you hear it from the kitchen but not the bedroom, the pergola louvers oriented to the afternoon sun and the neighbor's second-story windows, the planting chosen to look this way in year five, not just week one. None of that happens when a crew is squeezing you in between emergency jobs.

We're not the firm you call for a patio this weekend. We're the one you call when you want it right.

The selections:
• Arterra large-format porcelain pavers with gravel joints
• Bobe copper water bowl
• StruXure louvered pergola
• Eldorado Stone built-in bench
• olive, bougainvillea, rosemary & feather grass
• FX Luminaire path lighting
